title: Detection of Default Account Abuse Across Platforms
shortTitle: Detection of Default Account Abuse Across Platforms
summary: This strategy detects abuse of built-in default accounts such as Administrator, Guest and vendor-supplied service logins. It covers the default accounts technique under valid accounts, where an adversary never needs to create a user because a preinstalled one with a known or unchanged password already exists. The telemetry that makes it possible is authentication logging: Windows Security logon events, cloud identity sign-in logs and Linux or appliance authentication records, all joined to an inventory of which accounts are expected to log on where. In practice the strategy fails in two ways: environments that never disable or rename defaults generate constant noise, and service accounts that legitimately log on across many hosts blur the line between expected automation and credential abuse.

beginner.definition: This detection looks for logins that use the accounts a system or product creates for you. Examples are Administrator on Windows, root on Linux, and admin on many network devices. These accounts often ship with a known name, and sometimes with a known password that nobody changed.
beginner.whyItMatters: Default accounts are tempting because they already exist and need no malware to use. Many of them cannot be locked out the way a normal user can. If nobody monitors them, an intruder can sign in quietly for weeks. Watching them is a cheap way to catch stolen or guessed credentials early.
howItWorks: Your systems send authentication events to a central collection service, for example a Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) platform.
The detection keeps a list of default and built-in account names, such as Administrator, Guest and root.
It checks each successful or failed logon against that list.
It adds context, such as which machine the logon came from and whether that machine is unusual for this account.
It raises an alert when a default account logs on from a new host at an odd hour.
An analyst reviews the alert with the asset owner before treating it as an incident.
beginner.example: Think of an office building where every door has a master key hidden above the frame. Most staff ignore it, but a thief who knows the trick can walk in without breaking anything. The door log still records a key being used at two in the morning. This detection is the guard who reads that log and asks why the key was used.
takeaways: Default accounts are preinstalled, well known and often shipped with weak or shared passwords.
A successful logon by one of these accounts is only interesting when the host, time or volume is unusual.
Disabling or renaming defaults removes the risk, but monitoring them still catches missed cases.

objectives: Explain what a default account is and give three examples found in enterprise systems.
Identify the authentication telemetry that records default account use on Windows, Linux and cloud platforms.
Distinguish a routine service logon from credential abuse by comparing host, time and frequency.
Build a baseline of where each default account is expected to authenticate.
Describe the first three triage steps after a default account alert fires.
dataSources: Windows Security event 4624 successful logon and 4625 failed logon with target username and source workstation
Windows Security event 4672 special privileges assigned to a new logon
Linux authentication records from the system log or journal covering sshd and local console logons
Cloud identity provider sign-in logs showing user principal name, source IP address and client application
An asset inventory or configuration management database listing expected service accounts and their hosts
logic: The pattern is authentication as a built-in or vendor-default account from a context where that account is not expected. Start from successful logon events and failed logon events, keep the target username, the source workstation or source IP address, the logon type and the timestamp, then drop every account name that appears in the approved inventory for that host. What remains is suspicious when the source host is not in the account's normal set, when the logon happens outside a maintenance window, or when the same account suddenly authenticates to many hosts in a short period. The benign case is a service account logging on from a known automation server on a predictable schedule, so the correlation of account, source, destination and time is what separates the two.
pseudoQuery:
# title: Default Account Logon from Unexpected Source
# logsource:
#   product: windows
#   service: security
# detection:
#   selection:
#     EventID: 4624
#     TargetUserName|endswith:
#       - 'Administrator'
#       - 'Guest'
#     LogonType:
#       - 3
#       - 10
#   filter_expected:
#     SourceWorkstation|endswith:
#       - 'MGMT-JUMP01'
#       - 'BACKUP-SRV02'
#   condition: selection and not filter_expected
# level: high
falsePositives: Backup or disaster recovery software that signs in with the built-in local Administrator account on member servers each night
Vulnerability scanners and patch management agents that authenticate with a shared local administrator credential across a server subnet
Vendor remote support sessions that use a documented default maintenance account during an approved change window
Legacy applications and database links that still run under a renamed or unchanged built-in service account
tuningNotes: Start by building an inventory of default and built-in accounts on every platform, then map each one to the source hosts and time windows where it normally appears and express that as filter entries rather than deleting the rule. Scope the strictest version of the rule to internet-facing hosts, domain controllers and network devices, where a default account logon should almost never happen. Baseline failed logon volume per account before you set any threshold so that a normal password change on a service account does not look like password spraying. The coverage you lose by narrowing to specific hosts and accounts is insight into slow, low-volume abuse of defaults on developer laptops and lab systems, so keep a low-severity version of the rule running everywhere for hunting.
